questions.q: A 45-year-old patient with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis is being evaluated for biologic therapy. Genetic studies reveal a polymorphism in the IL-23R gene. Which statement best explains why IL-23 inhibitors targeting the p19 subunit are preferred over anti-p40 agents like ustekinumab?
opts: Anti-p40 agents block both IL-12 and IL-23, but IL-23—not IL-12—is the primary pathogenic driver of psoriasis
Anti-p40 agents have a shorter half-life and require more frequent dosing intervals
IL-23R polymorphisms are only responsive to p19-specific targeting, whereas p40 inhibition cannot engage these variants
Anti-p40 agents cause severe immunosuppression by blocking both Th1 and Th17 pathways simultaneously
questions.exp: Genome-wide association scans demonstrated that IL-23R polymorphisms are linked to psoriasis susceptibility, and mice deficient in IL-23 (but not IL-12) are highly resistant to autoimmune inflammation. Anti-p40 agents block the shared p40 subunit common to both IL-12 and IL-23, thereby neutralizing both cytokines. However, since IL-23 is the primary driver of the Th17 axis and psoriatic pathogenesis, selective p19 targeting achieves superior efficacy without unnecessary IL-12 blockade.
questions.memory_palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture two CASTLES side-by-side: one labeled IL-12 (useless for psoriasis, guarded by USTI the ustekinumab knight), the other IL-23 (the TRUE VILLAIN, targeted directly by a SHINY P19 SWORD held by GUSELS and RISANK warriors). The IL-23 castle CRUMBLES instantly, but blocking BOTH castles (p40) is overkill.

questions.q: A 50-year-old lepromatous leprosy patient is noted to have progressive loss of eyebrows. In which direction does this madarosis characteristically progress?
opts: Medially from the inner canthus toward the outer brow
Laterally from the outer third of the brow progressing medially toward the inner brow
Superiorly from the lid margin upward toward the hair-bearing scalp
In a diffuse pattern affecting the entire brow simultaneously and uniformly
questions.exp: Eyebrow loss (superciliary madarosis) in lepromatous leprosy characteristically begins in the cooler, lateral third of the brow and progresses medially. This pattern reflects the preference of *M. leprae* for cooler peripheral tissues and represents direct bacillary infiltration of hair follicles in the adnexa.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with progressive reticulate hyperpigmentation on the neck and axillae, complete absence of fingerprints, and severe heat intolerance. Genetic testing reveals a nonsense mutation in the KRT14 gene on chromosome 17q11.2-q21. Which of the following best explains the pathophysiological mechanism underlying this condition?
opts: Autoimmune-mediated destruction of melanocytes triggered by circulating pathogenic antibodies
Structural and functional defect in basal layer keratinocytes leading to increased susceptibility to pro-apoptotic stimuli
HLA-associated T-cell mediated immune complex deposition in the dermal-epidermal junction
Primary defect in eccrine sweat gland innervation due to autonomic nervous system dysfunction
questions.exp:
Naegeli-Franceschetti-Jadassohn syndrome is an autosomal dominant ectodermal dysplasia caused by KRT14 mutations that result in keratinocyte apoptosis, NOT an autoimmune disease. The pathogenic mechanism involves structural keratin defects making epidermal cells susceptible to programmed cell death, with no autoimmune serology involvement or HLA associations.
🏰 Palace: Picture a CRUMBLING CASTLE (keratinocytes) made of BROKEN STONE (KRT14 mutation) that collapses from any breeze (pro-apoptotic stimulus) — not attacked by knights (antibodies), just structurally weak.

questions.q: A 3-week-old neonate presents with profuse, purulent, blood-tinged nasal discharge and a coppery-red maculopapular rash involving the palms and soles with characteristic desquamation. The mother had untreated primary syphilis during pregnancy. Which clinical feature is MOST specific for early congenital syphilis and distinguishes it from acquired secondary syphilis in adults?
opts: Syphilitic pemphigus with vesiculobullous lesions on palms and soles
Hepatosplenomegaly with jaundice
Snuffles with spirochete-laden discharge
Condylomata lata in intertriginous areas
questions.exp: Syphilitic pemphigus is a unique feature of early congenital syphilis that presents as a vesiculobullous eruption (often present at birth or shortly after), predominantly affecting the palms and soles—a presentation that is NOT characteristic of acquired secondary syphilis in adults. While snuffles, hepatosplenomegaly, and condylomata lata can occur in both early congenital and secondary adult syphilis, the vesiculobullous pemphigus is pathognomonic for the congenital form.

questions.q: A neonate born at 31 weeks' gestation presents with profoundly rigid, tightly adherent skin and severe respiratory distress within hours of birth. Genetic testing reveals homozygous mutations in the ZMPSTE24 gene. Which of the following best explains the molecular pathogenesis of this condition?
opts: Loss of zinc metallopeptidase function leads to accumulation of farnesylated prelamin A and nuclear lamina disruption
Autoimmune-mediated destruction of dermal collagen by HLA-associated mechanisms
Defective keratinocyte differentiation due to impaired epidermal-dermal signaling only
Primary inflammatory infiltration of the dermis leading to fibrosis
questions.exp: ZMPSTE24 encodes a zinc metallopeptidase essential for post-translational cleavage of farnesylated prelamin A into mature lamin A. Without this enzyme, toxic unprocessed prelamin A accumulates and structurally damages the nuclear lamina, disrupting DNA replication and RNA transcription. This molecular defect, not immune or inflammatory mechanisms, drives the catastrophic arrest of skin maturation during the second trimester.
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: A ZINC GUARDIAN (ZMPSTE24) stands at the NUCLEAR CASTLE GATES, chopping farnesylated TOXIC PRELAMIN A into harmless MATURE LAMIN A pieces. Without the guardian, toxic garbage piles up, the nuclear walls crumble, and the entire kingdom (skin) freezes in fetal development—a LETHAL LAMINOPATHY that respects NO HLA ALLIES.

questions.q: A 4-month-old boy presents with a port-wine stain over the left forehead and upper eyelid. MRI brain shows leptomeningeal angiomatosis ipsilateral to the facial lesion, and ophthalmology identifies early choroidal vascular malformation. Which genetic mechanism best explains this triad of findings in Sturge-Weber syndrome?
opts: Autosomal dominant germline mutation in GNAQ inherited from an affected parent
Somatic postzygotic GNAQ mutation (c.548G>A; p.Arg183Gln) occurring early in anterior neural crest development
X-linked recessive GNA11 mutation present in all somatic cells
Mitochondrial inheritance pattern affecting neural crest-derived tissues
questions.exp:
Sturge-Weber syndrome is caused by a somatic, non-heritable postzygotic GNAQ mutation (c.548G>A; p.Arg183Gln) that occurs very early in the anterior neural crest before widespread migration, explaining the simultaneous facial port-wine stain, leptomeningeal angiomatosis, and choroidal malformation. This is not an inherited condition; the mutation is present only in affected lesional tissue and the neural crest-derived mural cells that ensheathe cephalic vasculature. The mutation drives constitutive activation of the MAPK pathway leading to abnormal vascular morphogenesis.
🏰 Palace: Picture a GNAQ mutation HITTING THE NEURAL CREST (at the castle GATES during early construction)—the early timing explains why the FOREHEAD, BRAIN, and EYES all get the same faulty blueprint, like three rooms painted by one corrupted construction crew before they dispersed.

questions.q: During a slit-lamp examination of a multibacillary leprosy patient, you observe thickened, edematous corneal nerves appearing as 'beads on a string.' What is the significance of this finding?
opts: It indicates advanced corneal scarring and imminent blindness
It is a pathognomonic early ocular sign of lepromatous leprosy and a warning sign for further ocular involvement
It represents secondary bacterial keratitis colonizing an anesthetic cornea
It is a non-specific finding seen in all types of leprosy with equal frequency
questions.exp: Thickened, edematous corneal nerves presenting as 'beads on a string' are pathognomonic and often the earliest ocular sign of lepromatous leprosy, signaling direct bacillary invasion of the cornea and need for close monitoring. This finding precedes many other serious ocular complications and should prompt aggressive management to prevent progression.

questions.q: A pregnant woman with primary syphilis at 14 weeks of gestation receives adequate penicillin treatment. According to current evidence regarding fetal immunocompetence and prevention of irreversible stigmata, what is the expected outcome?
opts: Fetal infection is prevented because maternal treatment before 16–18 weeks of gestation almost always prevents fetal infection and subsequent irreversible stigmata
The fetus will develop late congenital syphilis stigmata despite maternal treatment due to early placental invasion
Maternal treatment at this stage prevents transmission in primary syphilis but not early latent syphilis
The fetus will develop snuffles and syphilitic pemphigus because fetal immunocompetence is already established at 14 weeks
questions.exp: Adequate maternal penicillin treatment before the 16th to 18th week of pregnancy almost always prevents fetal infection because the fetus does not become fully immunocompetent until approximately 18–20 weeks of gestation. Since the characteristic inflammatory tissue destruction and necrosis require fetal immune response, early treatment prevents both infection and the subsequent irreversible stigmata.

questions.q: A 35-year-old patient with penicillin allergy presents with genital ulcer disease suspected to be non-herpetic (syphilis + chancroid). According to NACO guidelines, which kit and regimen should be administered?
opts: NACO Kit 3 (White): Azithromycin 1 g stat + Benzathine Penicillin 2.4 MU IM
NACO Kit 4 (Blue): Azithromycin 1 g stat + Doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14–15 days
NACO Kit 5 (Red): Acyclovir 400 mg TDS for 7 days
NACO Kit 6 (Black): Doxycycline 100 mg BD + Azithromycin 1 g stat
questions.exp:
NACO Kit 4 (Blue) is specifically designated for non-herpetic GUD in penicillin-allergic patients and contains Azithromycin 1 g stat plus Doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14–15 days. Kit 3 (White) contains penicillin and is contraindicated in penicillin allergy. Kit 5 treats herpetic GUD only.
🏰 Palace: Picture a BLUE knight with a DOXYCYCLINE SHIELD avoiding a massive PENICILLIN BOMB (marked with a red X) in the castle's medical arsenal, protecting an allergic patient in the tower.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the classic clinical presentation timeline and the classic anatomical distribution in Sturge-Weber syndrome?
opts: Port-wine stain appears at age 2–3 years; neurological features present at birth; lesions typically involve the lower face and neck
Port-wine stain present at birth over the upper face (V1 territory); seizures and stroke-like episodes most often present within the first one to two years
Capillary malformation develops gradually during infancy; leptomeningeal involvement is asymptomatic and discovered only on screening MRI
Port-wine stain present at birth affecting the lower face; ocular glaucoma develops only after age 5 years
questions.exp:
Sturge-Weber syndrome presents with a port-wine stain that is congenital and typically involves the upper face over the ophthalmic (V1) territory, whilst neurological manifestations such as grand-mal seizures and stroke-like episodes most commonly manifest within the first one to two years of life. The ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomatosis and choroidal vascular malformation are also present from birth but may not cause symptoms until infancy.
🏰 Palace: The BABY is BORN with a PURPLE WINE STAIN on the FOREHEAD (upper face, V1)—but the SEIZURE PARTY doesn't start until the first TWO YEARS, when the brain angiomas wake up and cause trouble.

questions.q: A 52-year-old male with a history of upper respiratory symptoms and pulmonary infiltrates develops constitutional symptoms and cutaneous vasculitis. Laboratory studies reveal positive c-ANCA and elevated creatinine with red cell casts in urine. Which type of small-vessel vasculitis is most consistent with this clinical presentation?
opts: Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA)
Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA/Wegener's)
Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA)
IgA Vasculitis
questions.exp: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA) is characterized by necrotizing granulomatous inflammation of the upper and lower respiratory tract combined with necrotizing vasculitis and is associated with c-ANCA (cytoplasmic anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody). The constellation of respiratory involvement, glomerulonephritis, and systemic vasculitis is classic for GPA.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with urethral discharge. According to WHO syndromic management guidelines, what is the recommended dual therapy regimen to cover both Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis?
opts: Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM + Doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days
Cefixime 400 mg PO + Azithromycin 1 g PO stat
Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM stat + Azithromycin 1 g PO stat or Doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days
Metronidazole 2 g stat + Cefixime 400 mg PO
questions.exp:
WHO guidelines recommend dual therapy with Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM stat (or Cefixime 400 mg PO stat) plus Azithromycin 1 g PO stat or Doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days to cover both organisms. NACO simplifies this with Azithromycin 1 g + Cefixime 400 mg PO stat (Kit 1, Grey).
🏰 Palace: Imagine two GUNMEN in the castle—CEPHALO-WARRIOR (ceftriaxone) and AZITH-ARSONIST (azithromycin) standing back-to-back firing at two targets labeled GC and CT in the urethral throne room.

questions.q: Approximately 70% of tuberous sclerosis patients have no family history of the disease. Which statement best explains this epidemiological observation?
opts: The TSC genes have exceptionally high spontaneous mutation rates, with 60-75% of cases arising from de novo mutations rather than inherited transmission
TSC demonstrates incomplete penetrance in approximately 70% of affected families, preventing clinical manifestation across generations
The two TSC genes (TSC1 and TSC2) are located on sex chromosomes, restricting inheritance patterns in approximately 70% of cases
Genomic imprinting silences the TSC1 gene in the paternal allele in 70% of affected individuals, creating a functionally hemizygous state
questions.exp: Despite being autosomal dominant with high penetrance, TSC exhibits a remarkably high spontaneous mutation rate. Approximately 60-75% of all affected individuals represent sporadic cases resulting from de novo mutations rather than familial inheritance, explaining why most patients lack a family history of the disease.
questions.source: [DVL] Neurocutaneous Syndromes I - NF1, NF2, TSC - Tuberous Sclerosis Complex
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Picture a FORTRESS where 75% of new SOLDIERS (de novo mutations) are freshly recruited rather than inheriting armor from their PARENTS—most TSC patients storm the castle alone without family backup.

questions.q: A 6-month-old infant presents with recurrent blisters on the dorsal hands and feet triggered by minor trauma, along with severe photosensitivity. Genetic testing reveals a homozygous loss-of-function mutation in the FERMT1 gene. Which of the following best explains the pathophysiological mechanism underlying this condition?
opts: Autoimmune destruction of hemidesmosomes with IgG and IgA deposition at the basement membrane zone
Loss of kindlin-1, a focal adhesion protein that normally links actin filaments in basal keratinocytes to the extracellular matrix
Deficiency of type VII collagen resulting in exclusive subepidermal cleavage
Pathogenic antibodies against BP180 and BP230 causing chronic inflammation and keratinocyte lysis
questions.exp: Kindler Syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in FERMT1 (formerly KIND1), leading to absence of kindlin-1, a structural focal adhesion protein critical for linking actin cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix in basal keratinocytes. This is NOT an autoimmune condition; routine autoimmune serology and direct immunofluorescence are negative. The structural defect impairs keratinocyte adhesion, shape, polarity, proliferation, and motility.
questions.🏰 Palace: Imagine KINDLIN-1 as a CHAIN LINK in a castle fortress—when it breaks, the actin rope holding the stone knights (keratinocytes) to the moat below snaps, causing knights to tumble (blistering). No angry villagers (autoimmune cells) needed!

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with facial papules, seizures, and learning difficulties. Genetic testing reveals a TSC2 mutation on chromosome 16p13.3. Which of the following best explains why TSC2 mutations typically present with more severe disease compared to TSC1 mutations?
opts: TSC2 mutations occur de novo more frequently than TSC1 mutations
TSC2 encodes tuberin, a larger protein that is more critical to the TSC complex function; TSC2 mutations are 3.4-3.5 times commoner and associated with more severe systemic involvement
TSC1 mutations are located on a more accessible chromosomal region, making them easier to repair by cellular mechanisms
TSC2 mutations cause earlier disease onset, whereas TSC1 mutations manifest only in adulthood
questions.exp: TSC2 mutations are responsible for the majority of TSC cases (3.4-3.5:1 ratio over TSC1) and consistently correlate with a more severe phenotype. TSC2 encodes the larger 200-kDa tuberin protein, which plays a critical role in the TSC complex's tumor-suppressive function. Patients with TSC2 mutations typically exhibit more extensive multisystem hamartomas and greater clinical severity compared to TSC1 mutation carriers.
questions.source: [DVL] Neurocutaneous Syndromes I - NF1, NF2, TSC - Tuberous Sclerosis Complex

questions.q: Which of the following conditions is correctly matched with its primary site of neutrophilic infiltration?
opts: Subcorneal pustular dermatosis (Sneddon-Wilkinson disease) — subcutaneous fat lobules
Neutrophilic eccrine hidradenitis — eccrine sweat glands
Sweet's syndrome — epidermal subcorneal pustules
Intraepidermal neutrophilic IgA dermatosis — reticular dermis
questions.exp: Neutrophilic eccrine hidradenitis is a subcutaneous and appendageal neutrophilic dermatosis characterized by neutrophilic infiltration targeting eccrine sweat glands, frequently observed in chemotherapy patients. Subcorneal pustular dermatosis affects the epidermis; Sweet's syndrome affects the dermis; and IgA dermatosis affects the intraepidermis.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man with lepromatous leprosy presents with bilateral inability to close his eyelids, exposed corneas, and loss of corneal sensation. Which combination of cranial nerve involvement best explains this clinical presentation?
opts: Trigeminal nerve (V) causing lagophthalmos and corneal anesthesia
Facial nerve (VII) causing lagophthalmos and trigeminal nerve (V) causing corneal anesthesia
Facial nerve (VII) alone causing both lagophthalmos and corneal anesthesia
Trigeminal nerve (V) alone causing lagophthalmos and facial nerve (VII) causing anesthesia
questions.exp: Facial nerve (VII) damage to the zygomatic and temporal branches causes paralysis of the orbicularis oculi muscle, resulting in lagophthalmos. Simultaneously, involvement of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve (V) causes corneal hypoesthesia or anesthesia. The combination of an exposed eye and insensitive cornea creates a dangerous situation for secondary infections.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with palpable purpura on the lower extremities, arthralgia, and hematuria. Skin biopsy shows necrotizing vasculitis with IgA1-dominant immune deposits. According to the 2012 CHCC nomenclature, which vessel size category does this condition affect?
opts: Large vessels (aorta and major branches)
Medium vessels (visceral arteries and their branches)
Small vessels (arterioles, capillaries, and venules)
Variable vessels (arteries, veins, and capillaries of all sizes)
questions.exp: IgA Vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein Purpura) is classified as a small-vessel vasculitis that affects arterioles, capillaries, and venules, with characteristic IgA1-dominant immune deposits in the skin, gut, and glomeruli. Small-vessel vasculitis typically produces palpable purpura on dependent areas and glomerulonephritis.

questions.q: An 8-year-old child with Kindler Syndrome who presented with acral blistering and photosensitivity in infancy now shows progressive poikiloderma, widespread cutaneous atrophy with a striking 'cigarette paper-like' appearance on the hands and feet, and erosive gingivitis. At which anatomical level(s) does ultrastructural skin cleavage occur in this condition?
opts: Exclusively within the basal keratinocytes (intraepidermal cleavage only)
Mixed levels: simultaneously within basal keratinocytes, through the lamina lucida, and/or below the lamina densa
Exclusively through the lamina lucida (junctional cleavage only)
Exclusively below the lamina densa (sublaminar densa cleavage only)
questions.exp: Kindler Syndrome is pathognomonic within the Epidermolysis Bullosa spectrum for exhibiting MIXED LEVELS of skin cleavage. Upon minimal trauma, ultrastructural failure can occur simultaneously at three different anatomical planes: intraepidermal, through the lamina lucida, and sublaminar densa. This mixed cleavage pattern is the defining structural feature that distinguishes Kindler Syndrome as a unique fourth major category of EB (alongside EB Simplex, Junctional EB, and Dystrophic EB).
questions.🏰 Palace: Imagine a castle with THREE FLOORS COLLAPSING at once: basement knights (intraepidermal), middle moat bridge (lamina lucida), and dungeon stones (sublamina densa)—Kindler tears through ALL LEVELS, unlike other EB subtypes that fail at single floors!

questions.q: A 3-day-old infant with restrictive dermopathy dies from respiratory insufficiency. Which ethnic population carries an exceptionally high carrier frequency for this condition, with an estimated 1 in 21 individuals being heterozygous carriers?
opts: Ashkenazi Jewish populations of Eastern Europe
Old Colony (Dutch-German) Mennonite and Hutterite populations in North America, particularly South Dakota
Japanese populations of the Pacific islands
Sub-Saharan African populations with sickle cell trait
questions.exp: A specific shared founder mutation in ZMPSTE24 is highly prevalent in the Old Colony (Dutch-German) Mennonite and Hutterite populations in North America, where carrier status is exceptionally high—estimated up to 1 in 21 in Hutterite populations from South Dakota. This represents a classic example of founder effect in isolated religious communities with high consanguinity.
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: In a SOUTH DAKOTA HUTTERITE FARMSTEAD, 1 out of every 21 villagers carries the FOUNDER'S CURSE (ZMPSTE24 mutation)—a genetic ghost inherited from Old Colony Dutch-German ancestors. Picture a TIGHT-SKINNED BABY frozen in a grain silo at 31 weeks, unable to breathe because the nuclear envelope collapsed like rotting barn walls.

questions.q: A 2-month-old infant born to a mother with systemic lupus erythematosus presents with erythematous lesions on the face and scalp. On histopathology, vacuolar interface dermatitis and liquefaction degeneration of basal keratinocytes with subepidermal cleft formation are noted. Direct immunofluorescence shows IgG and C3 deposition at the dermal-epidermal junction. Which HLA allele is most strongly associated with fetal susceptibility to the cutaneous manifestations of neonatal lupus?
opts: HLA-DQB1*02 and HLA-DRB1*03
HLA-B27 and HLA-B51
HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8
HLA-A2 and HLA-Cw6
questions.exp: Fetal susceptibility to neonatal lupus erythematosus is strongly influenced by specific HLA alleles, particularly HLA-DQB1*02 and HLA-DRB1*03. Additional genetic risk involves polymorphisms in the promoter region of the TNF-α gene. These genetic factors govern the fetal MHC presentation of transplacental maternal autoantibodies. 🏰 Palace: In the castle's GENETIC VAULT, the royal guards are HLA-DQB1*02 and DRB1*03 sentries—when they're posted at the palace gates, they WELCOME the invading maternal IgG antibodies straight through to the dermal-epidermal junction treasure room.

questions.q: A geneticist is counseling the parents of a child diagnosed with Naegeli-Franceschetti-Jadassohn syndrome regarding inheritance pattern and distinguishing clinical features. Which statement CORRECTLY describes this condition and its allelic relationship?
opts: Autosomal recessive inheritance with two distinct hierarchical subtypes based on severity of hypohidrosis
Autosomal dominant inheritance caused by KRT14 mutations; characterized by reticulate hyperpigmentation that typically FADES during adolescence and complete absence of dermatoglyphics
X-linked dominant inheritance with persistent reticulate hyperpigmentation that worsens throughout adulthood
Autosomal dominant inheritance caused by mutations in the KRTAP gene with progressive nail dystrophy but preserved fingerprints
questions.exp:
Naegeli-Franceschetti-Jadassohn is autosomal dominant due to KRT14 mutations on chromosome 17q11.2-q21, with the pathognomonic feature being reticulate hyperpigmentation that notably FADES during adolescence combined with total loss of fingerprints (absent dermatoglyphics). The condition is not divided into subtypes but exists as part of an allelic spectrum with Dermatopathia Pigmentosa Reticularis, both caused by the same gene.
🏰 Palace: Imagine a TEENAGE KNIGHT wearing a FADING RETICULATED NET ARMOR that DISSOLVES during his journey to adulthood, with no fingerprints on his gloved hands — the signature mark of NFJ's peculiar fade.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male presents with painful nodules and ulcerations on his legs along with fever and arthralgia. Histopathology reveals a dense neutrophilic infiltrate within the papillary and reticular dermis without evidence of vasculitis. Based on the anatomic depth of the infiltrate, which category of neutrophilic dermatosis is most likely?
opts: Primarily epidermal neutrophilic dermatosis
Primarily dermal neutrophilic dermatosis
Primarily subcutaneous and appendageal neutrophilic dermatosis
Mixed epidermal-dermal neutrophilic dermatosis
questions.exp: The classification of neutrophilic dermatoses is based on the primary anatomic depth of the neutrophilic infiltrate within the skin. Dense infiltrates in the papillary and reticular dermis characterize primarily dermal neutrophilic dermatoses, which represents the largest category and includes conditions like Sweet's syndrome and pyoderma gangrenosum.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman with lepromatous leprosy develops a corneal ulcer that grows progressively despite topical antibiotics and antifungals. Which statement best explains why conventional antimicrobial therapy is failing?
opts: Mycobacterium leprae has inherent resistance to all topical antimicrobials used in ophthalmology
The ulcer is caused by secondary bacterial or fungal infection of an undetected abrasion on an anesthetic, exposed cornea—not direct M. leprae invasion
The patient's immune system in lepromatous leprosy prevents any medication from reaching the cornea
Leprous pannus formation seals off blood supply, preventing drug penetration to infected tissue
questions.exp: Corneal ulcers in leprosy are not caused directly by *M. leprae* but by secondary bacterial or fungal infections colonizing undetected abrasions on an anesthetic, exposed cornea. Because the cornea lacks sensation (from trigeminal nerve involvement) and the eyelids cannot close properly (from facial nerve involvement), minor trauma goes unnoticed and becomes secondarily infected.

questions.q: A neonate presents at 6 weeks of age with characteristic erythematous, arcuate lesions distributed around the periorbital area and scalp, creating a distinctive facial appearance. The mother has a positive Ro/SSA antibody status. Which of the following best explains the pathophysiological mechanism underlying this cutaneous manifestation?
opts: Transplacental passage of maternal IgG autoantibodies against Ro-SSA and La-SSB targeting the dermal-epidermal junction
Active neonatal immune response against paternal HLA antigens in the skin
Neonatal T-cell mediated delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction to maternal IgM complexes
Passive transfer of maternal IgE autoantibodies causing mast cell degranulation in the dermis
questions.exp: Cutaneous neonatal lupus is caused by transplacental passage of maternal IgG1 autoantibodies directed against Ro-SSA (present in >90% of cutaneous NLE cases) and La-SSB, which target the dermal-epidermal junction and follicular epithelium. The characteristic 'owl eyes' or 'raccoon eyes' appearance results from confluence of lesions around the periorbital region. 🏰 Palace: Picture a MOTHER OWL flying through the PLACENTA carrying IgG antibodies like tiny eggs, depositing them in baby's DERMAL-EPIDERMAL JUNCTION—creating owl-masked babies staring back at the palace.

questions.q: A 10-day-old neonate presents with grouped vesicles on the scalp at the site of fetal scalp electrode placement, conjunctivitis, and oral ulcers. The CSF is normal and there is no evidence of hepatic involvement. Which neonatal HSV classification best describes this clinical presentation?
opts: Congenital intrauterine HSV infection
Skin-Eye-Mouth (SEM) disease
Disseminated HSV infection
CNS HSV infection without dissemination
questions.exp: SEM disease presents between days 1–2 weeks of life (classically days 9–11) with grouped vesicles on erythematous base affecting skin, eyes (keratoconjunctivitis), and mouth (ulcerative stomatitis), while visceral organs and CNS remain spared (normal CSF). The scalp electrode site represents typical site predilection. Mortality for isolated SEM is 0%, but untreated disease risks progression to CNS or disseminated involvement.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine three SPOTLIGHTS (Skin-Eye-Mouth) scanning a CASTLE at DAY 10, with VESICLES clustered on the SCALP ELECTRODE MARK, while the DUNGEON (CNS) and TREASURY (liver) remain DARK and SAFE—the TRIPLE THREAT without SYSTEMIC SIEGE.

questions.q: A mother presents in active labour at 38 weeks gestation with a primary genital HSV infection diagnosed two weeks ago. What is the approximate risk of neonatal HSV transmission?
opts: Less than 1% to 3%
questions.exp: Primary maternal genital HSV infection acquired near delivery (third trimester) carries a catastrophic 30–50% transmission risk due to high viral shedding and absence of protective transplacental maternal antibodies. In contrast, recurrent maternal herpes at delivery carries less than 1–3% risk. Critically, 70–90% of infected neonates are born to asymptomatic mothers with no known history.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a PREGNANT MOTHER holding a GLOWING ORB (30-50% transmission) that EXPLODES near the CASTLE GATES (primary infection at delivery), contrasting with a SLEEPING MOTHER whose DORMANT SHIELD blocks 97% of invaders (recurrent infection <1-3% risk).

questions.q: Risankizumab differs from guselkumab in which of the following pharmacokinetic parameters?
opts: Risankizumab has a significantly higher subcutaneous bioavailability (approximately 89% vs. 49%)
Guselkumab has a longer mean half-life (12–19 days vs. 8–12 days for risankizumab)
Risankizumab requires intravenous administration, whereas guselkumab is given subcutaneously
Guselkumab achieves maximum serum concentration faster than risankizumab after subcutaneous dosing
questions.exp: Risankizumab demonstrates excellent subcutaneous bioavailability of approximately 89%, whereas guselkumab has an estimated bioavailability of only 49%. Both are humanized/fully human IgG1 monoclonal antibodies targeting p19, but risankizumab's superior bioavailability contributes to more predictable serum concentrations and potentially more consistent clinical outcomes.
questions.memory_palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine RISANK (Risankizumab) as a CONFIDENT KNIGHT in gleaming armor walking DIRECTLY into the castle gate with 89% stride (HIGH BIOAVAILABILITY), while GUSELS (Guselkumab) sneaks in through a hidden tunnel at only 49% efficiency. RISANK's GOLDEN SHIELD = SUPERIOR ABSORPTION.
